rationale: A wins because it keeps the story honest while still giving the founder three pitchable roads: the no-show data, the studio-operator story, and the AI-pricing decision. Its strongest move is "Why Mindbody isn't charging extra for AI," which finds a real business angle in the supplied pricing fact. B has useful bones, but "Mindbody owns both the studio's booking system and ClassPass — now its AI sits on top of both" leans too hard on an implied product connection it later admits may not exist.
gaps_in_A: "Why Mindbody isn't charging extra for AI" is a strong angle, but it needs competitor pricing or retention context before it becomes more than smart inference.
"What an empty spot costs a boutique studio" asks for dollar impact, but the update supplies no revenue-per-spot figure; A handles this as proof needed, but the angle depends on getting it.

The refused line "If Mindbody will publish cross-studio numbers, this becomes the strongest angle" is useful, but it slightly over-promises without knowing whether the dataset is clean or representative.
gaps_in_B: "using aggregated booking data across the network" is invented. The update says booking data, not aggregated network data.
"now its AI sits on top of both" is too cute by half. The facts do not say the assistant touches ClassPass, and B builds a whole platform-power angle on that fog.
"distinct from the founder/category/competitor cuts below" is leftover angle-generator scaffolding; there is no founder angle here and no real competitor angle.
B misses A's cleaner pricing angle even though "pricing is bundled into existing software tiers" is one of the most pitchable business facts in the update.
